topics: ⚖️ Could the Patriarchs Withstand Strict Judgment? — the limits of rebuke, and whether a generation follows its leader
📜 New Chapter, New Mishna: Four Governing Principles — who determines affordability, age, and sex in a valuation vow
💰 Poor-Then-Rich, or Rich-Then-Poor — which rate applies at final payment?
🩹 Arakhin vs. a Leper's Offering — whose means actually count?
💸 Windfalls Don't Count for a Leper's Offering — only his ACTUAL current means matter

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Whose Means Determine the Payment?
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 17a–17b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf closes the discussion of rebuke with Rabbi Eliezer the Great's teaching that even the patriarchs could not withstand God's strict judgment, and a debate over whether a generation's character follows its leader or the reverse, resolved as a question of temperament rather than righteousness. A new mishna then opens the tractate's next chapter with four governing principles for a valuation vow: affordability follows the one who vows, while the age- and sex-based sum follows the person being valuated, fixed at the moment the vow is spoken. The Gemara contrasts this with vowing to provide a leper's purification offering, which follows the leper's own means rather than the vower's — except according to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who applies the 'follow the original subject's obligation' principle to valuations too. A further mishna addresses a change in financial status between the vow and its payment, ruling that the more stringent, wealthy rate always applies — in sharp contrast to a leper's own offering, which tracks only his actual possessions at the moment of payment.

slides.title: ⚖️ Could the Patriarchs Withstand Strict Judgment?
slides.subtitle: Closing the discussion of rebuke
slides.label: Rabbi Eliezer the Great teaches:
slides.text: Even Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob could not have withstood God's rebuke had He entered into strict judgment with them — proven from Samuel's own words, 'that I may plead with you...concerning all the righteous acts (i.e., mercies) of the Lord.' A separate debate asks whether a generation's level follows its leader, or a leader's level follows his generation — resolved not as a claim about righteousness (since righteous Zedekiah led an unrighteous generation, and wicked Jehoiakim an upright one) but about harshness versus gentleness of temperament.

slides.title: 📜 New Chapter, New Mishna: Four Governing Principles
slides.subtitle: Whose circumstances set the terms of a valuation vow?

boxes.title: Follows the VOWER
items: Affordability (heseg yad) — a poor person valuating a rich person pays only the poor rate, and a rich person valuating a poor person pays the rich rate

boxes.title: Follows the ONE VALUATED
items: The age-based fixed sum — set by the subject's own age
The male/female distinction — follows the subject, not the vower

boxes.title: Fixed at the Moment
items: The valuation amount locks in based on the subject's age and status AT THE TIME the vow is spoken

slides.title: 💰 Poor-Then-Rich, or Rich-Then-Poor — Which Rate Applies?
slides.subtitle: The mishna's rule, and Rabbi Yehuda's extension

lines.speaker: Tanna Kamma
lines.text: If one was poor when he vowed and became rich by payment time, OR was rich when he vowed and became poor by payment time — either way, he pays the RICH rate.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Derived from two phrases: rich-then-poor from 'according to the vower's means' (rich at the vow); poor-then-rich from 'al pi asher tasig' — the moment he speaks it with his mouth, or ultimately affords it.

lines.speaker: Rabbi Yehuda
lines.text: Even poor-then-rich-then-poor AGAIN — he still pays the rich rate, since 'if he is poor' requires unbroken poverty from start to finish.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: But shouldn't that same logic apply to a leper's OWN offering too? Yet a mishna in Nega'im says his status is fixed by only ONE of his offerings (sin, guilt, or the birds — disputed), regardless of fluctuation in between!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: The leper's own case rests on a distinct verse and is a special Torah edict — it does not require unbroken poverty. Only laws like the valuation vow demand consistency throughout.

slides.title: 🩹 Arakhin vs. a Leper's Offering — Whose Means Count?
slides.subtitle: Two vows that sound alike but follow opposite rules

boxes.title: Valuation Vow (Erech)
items: Follows the VOWER'S means — a poor person who valuates a rich person pays only the poor rate

boxes.title: Vowing to Provide a Leper's Offering
items: Follows the LEPER'S OWN means, not the vower's — a poor person who vows for a WEALTHY leper still brings the wealthy offering

callout.label: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi dissents:
callout.text: Even for arakhin he holds 'we follow the original subject's obligation' — so if a wealthy person vows his own valuation and a poor bystander adopts that vow ('what he said, upon me'), the poor bystander must still pay the WEALTHY rate.

slides.title: 💸 Windfalls Don't Count for a Leper's Offering
slides.subtitle: Current possession, not anticipated wealth, determines the sum
rows: One vowed his own valuation while poor, then inherited a fortune before paying
Pays the RICH rate — locked in by his status at the eventual moment of payment
A leper's father dies leaving him a fortune, or his cargo ship is about to arrive, before he brings his offering
NO effect — he still brings the offering matching his CURRENT actual possessions, not his anticipated wealth

summary.principle: The mishna carefully distinguishes whose circumstances govern a payment: a valuation vow tracks the vower's own means and locks in the more stringent rate across any change in fortune, while a leper's own purification offering tracks only his actual current possessions, indifferent to wealth already promised but not yet received.

flowSteps.content: ⚖️ Even the patriarchs couldn't withstand strict judgment; a leader/generation debate resolves to temperament, not righteousness
📜 New mishna: affordability follows the vower; age/sex follow the one valuated, fixed at the moment of the vow

columns.content: 💰 Poor↔rich fluctuation: the mishna always applies the RICH rate; R' Yehuda extends this even through a second dip to poor
🩹 A leper's own offering ignores fluctuation entirely and windfalls not yet received — only present possessions count

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: the Torah locates the relevant 'means' precisely — sometimes the vower's, sometimes the subject's, sometimes only the exact moment of payment — and never assumes wealth not yet in hand

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Eliezer the Great, what would have happened had God entered into strict judgment with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob?
o: They would have easily withstood it, since they were entirely righteous
They would not have been able to withstand the rebuke, since God actually dealt with them through mercy rather than the strict letter of the law
God would never have created the world
The question is left unresolved in the Gemara
quiz.e: Rabbi Eliezer the Great derives from Samuel's words about God's 'righteous acts' (i.e., mercies) toward the patriarchs that they were treated leniently, implying that strict judgment would have been unbearable even for them.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, whose financial means determine 'affordability' (heseg yad) in a valuation vow?
o: The person being valuated (the subject of the vow)
The one who takes the vow (the vower), not the person being valuated
The Temple treasurer
Both parties equally, split down the middle
quiz.e: The mishna states plainly that affordability is determined by the vower's means, derived from the verse 'according to the means of him who vowed.'

quiz.q: How does vowing to provide a leper's purification offering differ from a standard valuation vow, according to the mishna?
o: There is no difference; both follow the same rule
It follows the LEPER's own means, not the means of the person who vowed to provide it — the opposite of a valuation vow, which follows the vower's means
It always requires the wealthy-tier offering regardless of anyone's means
Only priests may vow to provide a leper's offering
quiz.e: The mishna explicitly contrasts the two: valuations track the vower's means, but a leper's offering tracks the leper's own actual financial status.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, if one was poor when he took a valuation vow and became wealthy by the time of payment (or vice versa), which rate does he pay?
o: The poor rate, in either case
The wealthy rate, in either case
An average of the two rates
Whichever rate is lower at each stage separately
quiz.e: The mishna rules that in both directions of change — poor-to-rich or rich-to-poor — the more stringent, wealthy rate applies.

quiz.q: Why does a leper's offering NOT increase even if he is about to inherit a large fortune or receive valuable cargo before actually bringing the offering?
o: Because leprosy offerings are always fixed regardless of wealth
Because his offering is determined solely by his actual, current possessions at the time he brings it, not by anticipated future wealth
Because the Temple treasury refuses windfall-based payments on principle
Because such windfalls are considered stolen property
quiz.e: The mishna states that even known future wealth — an inheritance or incoming cargo — has no bearing on the leper's offering, since only his present actual possessions determine what he brings.
